brief.situation: You are the cloud security engineer at Fernhill Analytics, a fictional company whose staff use Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365. At 09:05 an alert says three finance users consented to 'Invoice Sync Pro', an app from an unverified publisher, after a phishing email went to 40 finance and procurement staff. The app is already reading their mail and files. Users can still consent to any app. Investigate, contain, keep the evidence, and report.
handover: No administrator has approved this app; the grants are user consents.
Accounts payable pays supplier invoices that arrive by email.
howItWorks: Each task takes analyst time: choose it, then let the work finish, which moves the clock by the minutes that task takes. The attacker keeps working on the same clock.
New alerts and log lines appear in the console as they happen.
When you declare the incident contained, you notify, write the record and explain your reasoning.

writeup.question: For the incident report: how the attacker got access without a password, how you scoped it, what you did to cut it off and in what order, and what stops the next consent phish.

parts.label: How access was gained and scoped
parts.criteria: Explains that users granted delegated permissions (Mail.Read, Files.Read.All, offline_access) to an unverified app by consent, so no password was stolen; scopes from the consent audit entries (user consents, IsAdminContent False) and the app's current permissions list, noting the audit search lags.
parts.modelAnswer: Phished users clicked an OAuth consent prompt and granted the app delegated read access to mail and files with offline_access. The audit log showed user consents (IsAdminContent False); because audit entries can lag by 30 minutes or more, I took the current user list from the app's Permissions page.

parts.label: Containment
parts.criteria: Disables the app (not deletes it), removes its grants, revokes the users' sessions, restricts user consent, and warns accounts payable because harvested invoices enable payment fraud.
parts.modelAnswer: I disabled sign-in for the app so it gets no new tokens and no one can consent again, removed its delegated grants, revoked the users' refresh tokens, restricted user consent, and warned accounts payable to hold bank-detail changes. Deleting would have let the next consent bring it back.

parts.label: Prevention
parts.criteria: User consent limited to verified publishers and low-impact permissions with an admin consent workflow, plus periodic review of consented apps.
parts.modelAnswer: User consent is now limited to verified publishers and low-impact permissions, everything else goes through admin consent requests, and consented apps are reviewed on a schedule.

expertPath.text: Open the enterprise app's permissions and sign-ins: the current list of users who consented, the delegated scopes, the source address.
Disable user sign-in for the app: no new tokens, no new consents. Do not delete it.
Remove its grants, revoke the users' sessions, restrict user consent, and warn accounts payable to hold bank-detail changes.
Export audit records, sign-ins and grants; then the audit search to confirm scope as entries arrive.

contained.headline: Good: contained before it spread
contained.body: Consent phishing needs no password. You disabled the app, cut its grants and the users' sessions, closed consent, warned payments and kept the evidence.

containedLate.headline: Contained, with gaps
containedLate.body: The app is cut off. The criteria show what slipped: time, more consents, a deleted app that came back, or a step missed.

fraudPaid.headline: Payment fraud
fraudPaid.body: Mail access is a means to an end: invoices in the mailbox make convincing bank-change requests. Disable the app early and warn accounts payable.

stillIn.headline: Closed too soon
stillIn.body: While the app holds working grants it can read the users' mail. Disable it and remove the grants before closing.

time_up.headline: Time up
time_up.body: No record was written before the run's hard limit.

scoring.modelReasoning: Users granted an unverified app delegated Mail.Read, Files.Read.All and offline_access by consent, so the attacker needs no password. Scope from the app's current permissions (the audit search lags), disable the app's sign-in so it gets no new tokens and no one can consent again (deleting lets the next consent bring it back), remove its grants, revoke the users' sessions, restrict user consent to verified publishers and low-impact permissions, warn accounts payable about bank-detail changes, and export the evidence.
